Comping rhythms

Every comping rhythm the band plays, each built up a step at a time

A lesson for every comping rhythm the Backing Track band plays: built up from simpler ones, played on the band and written out as it plays.

All the accompaniment patterns · each lesson below is a section of this page; the list on the right jumps to one.

Varied

For piano or guitar, built up a step at a time.

This is a lesson on one comping rhythm the Backing Track band plays: Varied. It is built up from 3 simpler patterns, one step at a time, and every step is played by the band and written out as it plays. How the examples work: press ▶ Play, switch players in and out with the buttons beside it, and read what the band will play on the staff underneath: the whole pass is written out when Play starts, before it sounds. The tempo slider at the bottom of the page slows everything down.

All the accompaniment patterns

The pattern

The band chooses: two-bar phrases built from the swing figures, with some bars left empty. In straight eighths it plays the boogaloo stabs. Tick rhythms under it and it varies between just those.

It belongs in Swing, Jazz ballad and Boogaloo. Here it is in the swing style with the whole band. Switch the other players off to hear it alone.

Step 1: Charleston

Start with something simpler. A held chord on beat 1 and a short one on the and of 2. The first comping rhythm most players learn.

This is a pattern of its own: the lesson on it takes it further. Here it is only a step on the way, slowly. The drums keep time with you; switch the others on when it is steady.

Step 2: Reverse Charleston

The Charleston displaced: a short chord on the and of 1 and a held one on beat 3.

This is a pattern of its own: the lesson on it takes it further. Here it is only a step on the way, slowly. The drums keep time with you; switch the others on when it is steady.

Step 3: Red Garland

Chords on the and of 2 and the and of 4. The second one anticipates the next bar’s chord and is held across the barline.

This is a pattern of its own: the lesson on it takes it further. Here it is only a step on the way, slowly. The drums keep time with you; switch the others on when it is steady.

Step 4: Varied, slowly

Now the pattern itself. Compare it with the step before: press each button while the band plays and watch what changes on the staff.

How to play it. Real comping mixes the figures you have learned: two-bar phrases, some bars left empty. Choose one figure per bar and vary it; leave space for the soloist.

The band plays it on piano here; the step after next has it on guitar.

Step 5: Up to tempo, with the band

The whole band, at 120 beats a minute. Play along, then switch the band’s chord player off and take the part yourself.

Step 6: On the guitar

The same rhythm on the guitar. On guitar each chord is a strum or a pluck of a chord shape; a short chord is choked by easing the fretting hand off the strings.

Step 7: Two chords in a bar

Harder: now some bars have two chords, two beats each. The pattern keeps its rhythm and changes chord where the bar does: watch the staff for the hit that lands on beat 3.

In other styles

The same comping rhythm in other styles it fits. The other players change; yours does not. Notice how the same part sounds different in a different band.

Jazz ballad

Boogaloo

  • Builds on: Charleston, Reverse Charleston, Red Garland.
  • Plays with, in swing: Walking (bass line), Jazz time (drum groove).
  • Other comping rhythms in the Jazz group: Charleston, Reverse Charleston, Red Garland, Off-beats, Long notes, Four to the bar, Boogaloo stabs, Stride.

Charleston

For piano or guitar, built up a step at a time.

This is a lesson on one comping rhythm the Backing Track band plays: Charleston. It is built up from 2 simpler patterns, one step at a time, and every step is played by the band and written out as it plays. How the examples work: press ▶ Play, switch players in and out with the buttons beside it, and read what the band will play on the staff underneath: the whole pass is written out when Play starts, before it sounds. The tempo slider at the bottom of the page slows everything down.

All the accompaniment patterns

The pattern

A held chord on beat 1 and a short one on the and of 2. The first comping rhythm most players learn.

It belongs in Swing and Jazz ballad. Here it is in the swing style with the whole band. Switch the other players off to hear it alone.

Step 1: Long notes

Start with something simpler. One held chord per bar (or per chord). Leaves the most room for a soloist.

This is a pattern of its own: the lesson on it takes it further. Here it is only a step on the way, slowly. The drums keep time with you; switch the others on when it is steady.

Step 2: Quarter-note chords

The chord on every beat, held. On the piano the left hand adds the root underneath as each chord arrives: Let It Be, Imagine, Someone Like You.

This is a pattern of its own: the lesson on it takes it further. Here it is only a step on the way, slowly. The drums keep time with you; switch the others on when it is steady.

Step 3: Charleston, slowly

Now the pattern itself. Compare it with the step before: press each button while the band plays and watch what changes on the staff.

How to play it. A held chord on 1 and a short one on the and of 2 (swung). Say it: ONE … and. On piano, a rootless voicing in the left hand; on guitar, a three-note shape with the second chord choked.

The band plays it on piano here; the step after next has it on guitar.

Step 4: Up to tempo, with the band

The whole band, at 120 beats a minute. Play along, then switch the band’s chord player off and take the part yourself.

Step 5: On the guitar

The same rhythm on the guitar. On guitar each chord is a strum or a pluck of a chord shape; a short chord is choked by easing the fretting hand off the strings.

Step 6: Two chords in a bar

Harder: now some bars have two chords, two beats each. The pattern keeps its rhythm and changes chord where the bar does: watch the staff for the hit that lands on beat 3.

In other styles

The same comping rhythm in another style it fits. The other players change; yours does not. Notice how the same part sounds different in a different band.

Jazz ballad

How it relates to the other patterns

  • Builds on: Long notes, Quarter-note chords.
  • Leads to: Boogie-woogie right hand, Reverse Charleston, Off-beats, Red Garland, Varied, Boogaloo stabs, Take Five vamp, Bossa nova: the patterns that use this one as a step.
  • Plays with, in swing: Walking (bass line), Jazz time (drum groove).
  • Other comping rhythms in the Jazz group: Varied, Reverse Charleston, Red Garland, Off-beats, Long notes, Four to the bar, Boogaloo stabs, Stride.

The pattern

Step 2: Off-beats

Chords on the and of 1 and the and of 3, never on a downbeat.

This is a pattern of its own: the lesson on it takes it further. Here it is only a step on the way, slowly. The drums keep time with you; switch the others on when it is steady.

Step 3: Red Garland, slowly

Now the pattern itself. Compare it with the step before: press each button while the band plays and watch what changes on the staff.

How to play it. Chords on the and of 2 and the and of 4; the second one is the next bar’s chord, early, held across the barline. The anticipation pulls the band forward.

The band plays it on piano here; the step after next has it on guitar.

Long notes

For piano or guitar, built up a step at a time.

This is a lesson on one comping rhythm the Backing Track band plays: Long notes. It is one of the first patterns to learn, so this page starts from it and takes it into the band. How the examples work: press ▶ Play, switch players in and out with the buttons beside it, and read what the band will play on the staff underneath: the whole pass is written out when Play starts, before it sounds. The tempo slider at the bottom of the page slows everything down.

All the accompaniment patterns

The pattern

One held chord per bar (or per chord). Leaves the most room for a soloist.

It belongs in Swing, Jazz ballad, Boogaloo, Bossa nova, Tango, Piano ballad, Boom-chick, Straight-eighth rock, Reggaeton, Acoustic strum, Dance pop, 12/8 doo-wop, Hymn (four parts), Folk carol, Emo / pop-punk and John Prine Fingerpicking. Here it is in the piano ballad style with the whole band. Switch the other players off to hear it alone.

Step 1: Long notes, slowly

How to play it. One chord, struck once, held for the bar. On piano, play it and keep the keys down (or the pedal down) until the chord changes; on guitar, strum once and let it ring. Use it to learn the chords and the changes before any rhythm.

The band plays it on piano here; the step after next has it on guitar.

Step 2: Up to tempo, with the band

The whole band, at 72 beats a minute. Play along, then switch the band’s chord player off and take the part yourself.

Step 3: On the guitar

The same rhythm on the guitar. On guitar each chord is a strum or a pluck of a chord shape; a short chord is choked by easing the fretting hand off the strings.

Step 4: Two chords in a bar

Harder: now some bars have two chords, two beats each. The pattern keeps its rhythm and changes chord where the bar does: watch the staff for the hit that lands on beat 3.

Step 5: In 3/4

The same pattern in a waltz: three beats to the bar. Listen for what it keeps and what it drops when the bar is a beat shorter.

In other styles

The same comping rhythm in other styles it fits. The other players change; yours does not. Notice how the same part sounds different in a different band.

All the accompaniment patterns

The pattern

A short chord on every beat with 2 and 4 a little louder, the way Freddie Green played rhythm guitar.

It belongs in Swing, Boogie-woogie and Jump blues. Here it is in the swing style with the whole band. Switch the other players off to hear it alone.

Step 1: Long notes

Start with something simpler. One held chord per bar (or per chord). Leaves the most room for a soloist.

This is a pattern of its own: the lesson on it takes it further. Here it is only a step on the way, slowly. The drums keep time with you; switch the others on when it is steady.

Step 2: Quarter-note chords

The chord on every beat, held. On the piano the left hand adds the root underneath as each chord arrives: Let It Be, Imagine, Someone Like You.

This is a pattern of its own: the lesson on it takes it further. Here it is only a step on the way, slowly. The drums keep time with you; switch the others on when it is steady.

Step 3: Four to the bar, slowly

Now the pattern itself. Compare it with the step before: press each button while the band plays and watch what changes on the staff.

How to play it. A short chord on every beat, 2 and 4 a little louder, the way Freddie Green played. On guitar use three-note shapes on the middle strings and release the pressure right after each strum.

Step 4: Up to tempo, with the band

The whole band, at 120 beats a minute. Play along, then switch the band’s chord player off and take the part yourself.

Step 5: Two chords in a bar

Harder: now some bars have two chords, two beats each. The pattern keeps its rhythm and changes chord where the bar does: watch the staff for the hit that lands on beat 3.

All the accompaniment patterns

The pattern

A stab on beat 1, the chord pushed and held on the and of 2, and sometimes an answering stab late in the bar. Locks with the boogaloo bass riff.

It belongs in Boogaloo. Here it is in the boogaloo style with the whole band. Switch the other players off to hear it alone.

Step 1: Long notes

Start with something simpler. One held chord per bar (or per chord). Leaves the most room for a soloist.

This is a pattern of its own: the lesson on it takes it further. Here it is only a step on the way, slowly. The drums keep time with you; switch the others on when it is steady.

Step 2: Charleston

A held chord on beat 1 and a short one on the and of 2. The first comping rhythm most players learn.

This is a pattern of its own: the lesson on it takes it further. Here it is only a step on the way, slowly. The drums keep time with you; switch the others on when it is steady.

Step 3: Boogaloo stabs, slowly

Now the pattern itself. Compare it with the step before: press each button while the band plays and watch what changes on the staff.

How to play it. A stab on 1, the chord pushed and held on the and of 2, and sometimes an answer late in the bar. It locks with the boogaloo bass riff, which pushes on the same and of 2.

The band plays it on piano here; the step after next has it on guitar.

Step 4: Up to tempo, with the band

The whole band, at 112 beats a minute. Play along, then switch the band’s chord player off and take the part yourself.

Step 5: On the guitar

The same rhythm on the guitar. On guitar each chord is a strum or a pluck of a chord shape; a short chord is choked by easing the fretting hand off the strings.

Step 6: Two chords in a bar

Harder: now some bars have two chords, two beats each. The pattern keeps its rhythm and changes chord where the bar does: watch the staff for the hit that lands on beat 3.

How it relates to the other patterns

  • Builds on: Long notes, Charleston.
  • The same idea elsewhere in the band: Boogaloo riff (bass line), Boogaloo riff, walking at times (bass line), Funk (drum groove).
  • Plays with, in boogaloo: Boogaloo riff (bass line), Jazz time (drum groove), Tumbao (conga part).
  • Other comping rhythms in the Jazz group: Varied, Charleston, Reverse Charleston, Red Garland, Off-beats, Long notes, Four to the bar, Stride.

Stride

For piano, built up a step at a time.

This is a lesson on one comping rhythm the Backing Track band plays: Stride. It is built up from a simpler pattern, one step at a time, and every step is played by the band and written out as it plays. How the examples work: press ▶ Play, switch players in and out with the buttons beside it, and read what the band will play on the staff underneath: the whole pass is written out when Play starts, before it sounds. The tempo slider at the bottom of the page slows everything down.

All the accompaniment patterns

The pattern

The stride pianist’s left hand: a low bass note on beats 1 and 3 (the root in octaves where a chord starts, its fifth on beat 3) and the chord in the middle of the keyboard on beats 2 and 4. In 3/4 the bass on 1 and the chord on 2 and 3. On the guitar it is plain boom-chick.

It belongs in Stride piano and Ragtime. Here it is in the stride piano style with the whole band. Switch the other players off to hear it alone.

Step 1: Boom-chick / oom-pah-pah

Start with something simpler. Short chords on the beats the bass leaves free: 2 and 4 in 4/4, 2 and 3 in a waltz. Goes with the Root and fifth bass line.

This is a pattern of its own: the lesson on it takes it further. Here it is only a step on the way, slowly. The drums keep time with you; switch the others on when it is steady.

Step 2: Stride, slowly

Now the pattern itself. Compare it with the step before: press each button while the band plays and watch what changes on the staff.

How to play it. The left hand alone first: a low octave on the root on beat 1, a chord about two octaves higher on beat 2, the fifth down low on beat 3, the chord again on 4. Look at where the hand lands, not where it has been: the leap down is the hard one. Keep the bass notes short and the chords lighter. When it is steady, let the band’s bass and drums join.

Step 3: Up to tempo, with the band

The whole band, at 132 beats a minute. Play along, then switch the band’s chord player off and take the part yourself.

Step 4: Two chords in a bar

Harder: now some bars have two chords, two beats each. The pattern keeps its rhythm and changes chord where the bar does: watch the staff for the hit that lands on beat 3.

Step 5: In 3/4

The same pattern in a jazz waltz: three beats to the bar. Listen for what it keeps and what it drops when the bar is a beat shorter.

In other styles

The same comping rhythm in another style it fits. The other players change; yours does not. Notice how the same part sounds different in a different band.

Stride in tenths

For piano, built up a step at a time.

This is a lesson on one comping rhythm the Backing Track band plays: Stride in tenths. It is built up from 2 simpler patterns, one step at a time, and every step is played by the band and written out as it plays. How the examples work: press ▶ Play, switch players in and out with the buttons beside it, and read what the band will play on the staff underneath: the whole pass is written out when Play starts, before it sounds. The tempo slider at the bottom of the page slows everything down.

All the accompaniment patterns

The pattern

Stride with a wider left hand: on beat 1 a tenth (the root with the chord’s 3rd an octave above it, together); on beat 3 the fifth, or, when the chord is about to change, a tenth walking to a step from the next root. Chords in the middle of the keyboard on 2 and 4. A tenth that would crowd the chords is played as its low note alone. On the guitar it is plain boom-chick.

It belongs in Stride piano and Ragtime. Here it is in the stride piano style with the whole band. Switch the other players off to hear it alone.

Step 1: Boom-chick / oom-pah-pah

Start with something simpler. Short chords on the beats the bass leaves free: 2 and 4 in 4/4, 2 and 3 in a waltz. Goes with the Root and fifth bass line.

This is a pattern of its own: the lesson on it takes it further. Here it is only a step on the way, slowly. The drums keep time with you; switch the others on when it is steady.

Step 2: Stride

The stride pianist’s left hand: a low bass note on beats 1 and 3 (the root in octaves where a chord starts, its fifth on beat 3) and the chord in the middle of the keyboard on beats 2 and 4. In 3/4 the bass on 1 and the chord on 2 and 3. On the guitar it is plain boom-chick.

This is a pattern of its own: the lesson on it takes it further. Here it is only a step on the way, slowly. The drums keep time with you; switch the others on when it is steady.

Step 3: Stride in tenths, slowly

Now the pattern itself. Compare it with the step before: press each button while the band plays and watch what changes on the staff.

How to play it. The stride left hand, stretched: on beat 1 the root with the 3rd an octave above it, both at once (roll them if your hand will not reach). On beat 3 the fifth, or, before a chord change, a tenth a step away from the next root, so the bass walks into it. Learn the leaps first with single notes, then add the top of each tenth.

Step 4: Up to tempo, with the band

The whole band, at 132 beats a minute. Play along, then switch the band’s chord player off and take the part yourself.

Step 5: Two chords in a bar

Harder: now some bars have two chords, two beats each. The pattern keeps its rhythm and changes chord where the bar does: watch the staff for the hit that lands on beat 3.

In other styles

The same comping rhythm in another style it fits. The other players change; yours does not. Notice how the same part sounds different in a different band.

All the accompaniment patterns

The pattern

A two-bar riff of short swung chords against the walking left hand: beat 1, the and of 1 and the and of 2 (held); then the and of 1, beat 2 and the and of 3 (held).

It belongs in Boogie-woogie and Jump blues. Here it is in the boogie-woogie style with the whole band. Switch the other players off to hear it alone.

Step 1: Every off-beat

Start with something simpler. A short chord on the and of every beat and never on the beat: the ska and calypso afterbeat.

This is a pattern of its own: the lesson on it takes it further. Here it is only a step on the way, slowly. The drums keep time with you; switch the others on when it is steady.

Step 2: Charleston

A held chord on beat 1 and a short one on the and of 2. The first comping rhythm most players learn.

This is a pattern of its own: the lesson on it takes it further. Here it is only a step on the way, slowly. The drums keep time with you; switch the others on when it is steady.

Step 3: Boogie-woogie right hand, slowly

Now the pattern itself. Compare it with the step before: press each button while the band plays and watch what changes on the staff.

How to play it. Short chords against the walking bass, a two-bar riff: 1, the and of 1, the and of 2 held; then the and of 1, 2, the and of 3 held. Keep the right hand light and swung, and play the same riff on every chord of the blues: it does not need to change, the bass does the moving.

Step 4: Up to tempo, with the band

The whole band, at 132 beats a minute. Play along, then switch the band’s chord player off and take the part yourself.

Step 5: Two chords in a bar

Harder: now some bars have two chords, two beats each. The pattern keeps its rhythm and changes chord where the bar does: watch the staff for the hit that lands on beat 3.

All the accompaniment patterns

The pattern

A two-bar pattern. Nothing in the first bar, under the bass call. In the second, two chords: the voicing a whole step above the chord, held from beat 3, then the chord itself, short, on the and of 4. Use the Fourths voicing for the sound of the record.

It belongs in Swing. Here it is in the swing style with the whole band. Switch the other players off to hear it alone.

Step 1: Long notes

Start with something simpler. One held chord per bar (or per chord). Leaves the most room for a soloist.

This is a pattern of its own: the lesson on it takes it further. Here it is only a step on the way, slowly. The drums keep time with you; switch the others on when it is steady.

Step 2: Off-beats

Chords on the and of 1 and the and of 3, never on a downbeat.

This is a pattern of its own: the lesson on it takes it further. Here it is only a step on the way, slowly. The drums keep time with you; switch the others on when it is steady.

Step 3: So What: the answer, slowly

Now the pattern itself. Compare it with the step before: press each button while the band plays and watch what changes on the staff.

How to play it. Two bars: nothing in the first while the bass plays the call; in the second, a chord a whole step above held from 3, then the chord itself, short, on the and of 4. ‘So what.’

The band plays it on piano here; the step after next has it on guitar.

Step 4: Up to tempo, with the band

The whole band, at 132 beats a minute. Play along, then switch the band’s chord player off and take the part yourself.

Step 5: On the guitar

The same rhythm on the guitar. On guitar each chord is a strum or a pluck of a chord shape; a short chord is choked by easing the fretting hand off the strings.

Step 6: Two chords in a bar

Harder: now some bars have two chords, two beats each. The pattern keeps its rhythm and changes chord where the bar does: watch the staff for the hit that lands on beat 3.

How it relates to the other patterns

  • Builds on: Long notes, Off-beats.
  • The same idea elsewhere in the band: So What: the bass call (bass line).
  • Plays with, in swing: Walking (bass line), Jazz time (drum groove).
  • Other comping rhythms in the From tunes group: Maiden Voyage, Take Five vamp.

All the accompaniment patterns

The pattern

For a quick 3/4. The root on 1 and light, short chords on 2 and 3, the third beat the lighter. The bars go in fours: the first leans, the third a little, and the fourth grows into the next phrase. In 4/4 it is boom-chick.

It belongs in Waltz (in one), Boom-chick, Folk carol and Hymn (four parts). Here it is in the waltz (in one) style with the whole band. Switch the other players off to hear it alone.

Step 1: Long notes

Start with something simpler. One held chord per bar (or per chord). Leaves the most room for a soloist.

This is a pattern of its own: the lesson on it takes it further. Here it is only a step on the way, slowly. The drums keep time with you; switch the others on when it is steady.

Step 2: Boom-chick / oom-pah-pah

Short chords on the beats the bass leaves free: 2 and 4 in 4/4, 2 and 3 in a waltz. Goes with the Root and fifth bass line.

This is a pattern of its own: the lesson on it takes it further. Here it is only a step on the way, slowly. The drums keep time with you; switch the others on when it is steady.

Step 3: Waltz in one, slowly

Now the pattern itself. Compare it with the step before: press each button while the band plays and watch what changes on the staff.

How to play it. Root on 1, light short chords on 2 and 3, the third the lightest. It is felt in one: one big beat a bar. The four bars of a phrase lean, rest, lean a little, and grow into the next phrase.

The band plays it on piano here; the step after next has it on guitar.

Step 4: Up to tempo, with the band

The whole band, at 150 beats a minute. Play along, then switch the band’s chord player off and take the part yourself.

Step 5: On the guitar

The same rhythm on the guitar. On guitar each chord is a strum or a pluck of a chord shape; a short chord is choked by easing the fretting hand off the strings.

Ballad: rocking

For piano, built up a step at a time.

It is built up from 2 simpler patterns, one step at a time, and every step is played by the band and written out as it plays. All the accompaniment patterns

The pattern

Quarter notes: the chord on 1, the thumb on 2, the top two notes on 3, the thumb on 4, over held left-hand octaves on the root. On the piano with the Standard voicing the chord is a triad in first inversion.

It belongs in Piano ballad, Acoustic strum, Folk carol, Hymn (four parts) and 12/8 doo-wop. Here it is in the piano ballad style with the whole band. Switch the other players off to hear it alone.

Step 1: Quarter-note chords

Start with something simpler. The chord on every beat, held. On the piano the left hand adds the root underneath as each chord arrives: Let It Be, Imagine, Someone Like You.

This is a pattern of its own: the lesson on it takes it further. Here it is only a step on the way, slowly. The drums keep time with you; switch the others on when it is steady.

Step 2: Hymn: four parts

Every chord played once and held until the next one. On the piano or organ it is four parts: the root in the left hand and three voices above it that move as little as possible from chord to chord. It follows the chart’s chords, so a carol written with a chord on every beat sounds like the hymnal.

This is a pattern of its own: the lesson on it takes it further. Here it is only a step on the way, slowly. The drums keep time with you; switch the others on when it is steady.

Step 3: Ballad: rocking, slowly

Now the pattern itself. Compare it with the step before: press each button while the band plays and watch what changes on the staff.

How to play it. Left hand: an octave on the root, held. Right hand in quarter notes: the whole chord on 1, the thumb on 2, the top two notes on 3, the thumb on 4. The right hand rocks between the thumb and the top.

Step 4: Up to tempo, with the band

The whole band, at 72 beats a minute. Play along, then switch the band’s chord player off and take the part yourself.

Step 5: Two chords in a bar

Harder: now some bars have two chords, two beats each. The pattern keeps its rhythm and changes chord where the bar does: watch the staff for the hit that lands on beat 3.

The same comping rhythm in other styles it fits. The other players change; yours does not. Notice how the same part sounds different in a different band.

Step 1: Quarter-note chords

Start with something simpler. The chord on every beat, held. On the piano the left hand adds the root underneath as each chord arrives: Let It Be, Imagine, Someone Like You.

This is a pattern of its own: the lesson on it takes it further. Here it is only a step on the way, slowly. The drums keep time with you; switch the others on when it is steady.

Step 2: 3+3+2 (tresillo)

Three held chords in a bar of eight eighth notes, grouped 3+3+2: beat 1, the and of 2, beat 4. Clocks, Shape of You, Eye of the Tiger.

This is a pattern of its own: the lesson on it takes it further. Here it is only a step on the way, slowly. The drums keep time with you; switch the others on when it is steady.

Step 3: Ballad: syncopated, slowly

Now the pattern itself. Compare it with the step before: press each button while the band plays and watch what changes on the staff.

How to play it. Three sounds a bar grouped 3+3+2: the chord on 1, its top two notes on the and of 2 and on 4. Hold each one until the next. The left hand stays on the root octave.

Step 4: Up to tempo, with the band

The whole band, at 72 beats a minute. Play along, then switch the band’s chord player off and take the part yourself.

Step 5: Two chords in a bar

Harder: now some bars have two chords, two beats each. The pattern keeps its rhythm and changes chord where the bar does: watch the staff for the hit that lands on beat 3.

In other styles

The same comping rhythm in other styles it fits. The other players change; yours does not. Notice how the same part sounds different in a different band.

All the accompaniment patterns

The pattern

The chord on every beat, held. On the piano the left hand adds the root underneath as each chord arrives: Let It Be, Imagine, Someone Like You.

It belongs in Piano ballad, Straight-eighth rock, Acoustic strum, Motown / soul, Hymn (four parts), Folk carol and Emo / pop-punk. Here it is in the piano ballad style with the whole band. Switch the other players off to hear it alone.

Step 1: Long notes

Start with something simpler. One held chord per bar (or per chord). Leaves the most room for a soloist.

This is a pattern of its own: the lesson on it takes it further. Here it is only a step on the way, slowly. The drums keep time with you; switch the others on when it is steady.

Step 2: Quarter-note chords, slowly

Now the pattern itself. Compare it with the step before: press each button while the band plays and watch what changes on the staff.

How to play it. The chord on every beat. On piano: right hand plays the chord on each beat, left hand plays the root as the chord arrives. On guitar: four even downstrokes. Keep every chord the same loudness.

The band plays it on piano here; the step after next has it on guitar.

Step 3: Up to tempo, with the band

The whole band, at 72 beats a minute. Play along, then switch the band’s chord player off and take the part yourself.

Step 4: On the guitar

The same rhythm on the guitar. On guitar each chord is a strum or a pluck of a chord shape; a short chord is choked by easing the fretting hand off the strings.

Step 5: Two chords in a bar

Harder: now some bars have two chords, two beats each. The pattern keeps its rhythm and changes chord where the bar does: watch the staff for the hit that lands on beat 3.

Step 6: In 3/4

The same pattern in a waltz: three beats to the bar. Listen for what it keeps and what it drops when the bar is a beat shorter.

The same comping rhythm in other styles it fits. The other players change; yours does not. Notice how the same part sounds different in a different band.

The pattern

The notes of the chord one at a time in eighth notes: lowest, highest, middle, highest. Mozart’s Sonata K. 545.

It belongs in Piano ballad and Boom-chick. Here it is in the piano ballad style with the whole band. Switch the other players off to hear it alone.

Step 1: Hymn: four parts

Start with something simpler. Every chord played once and held until the next one. On the piano or organ it is four parts: the root in the left hand and three voices above it that move as little as possible from chord to chord. It follows the chart’s chords, so a carol written with a chord on every beat sounds like the hymnal.

This is a pattern of its own: the lesson on it takes it further. Here it is only a step on the way, slowly. The drums keep time with you; switch the others on when it is steady.

Step 2: Arpeggio, low and high

Eighth notes rocking between the lowest and the highest note of the voicing.

This is a pattern of its own: the lesson on it takes it further. Here it is only a step on the way, slowly. The drums keep time with you; switch the others on when it is steady.

Step 3: Alberti bass, slowly

Now the pattern itself. Compare it with the step before: press each button while the band plays and watch what changes on the staff.

How to play it. Lowest, highest, middle, highest, in even eighths. Keep the chord under the hand and let the fingers do the work: 5-1-3-1 in the left hand, or 1-5-3-5 in the right. Quiet and even, the way Mozart wrote it.

Step 4: Up to tempo, with the band

The whole band, at 72 beats a minute. Play along, then switch the band’s chord player off and take the part yourself.

Step 5: Two chords in a bar

Harder: now some bars have two chords, two beats each. The pattern keeps its rhythm and changes chord where the bar does: watch the staff for the hit that lands on beat 3.

Step 6: In 3/4

The same pattern in a waltz: three beats to the bar. Listen for what it keeps and what it drops when the bar is a beat shorter.

Step 2: Groups: 3+3+3+3+2+2

Sixteen eighth notes over two bars grouped 3+3+3+3+2+2. First bar (shown): 1, the and of 2, 4. Second bar: the and of 1, 3, 4. Beautiful Day.

This is a pattern of its own: the lesson on it takes it further. Here it is only a step on the way, slowly. The drums keep time with you; switch the others on when it is steady.

Step 3: Groups: 3+3+4+3+3, slowly

Now the pattern itself. Compare it with the step before: press each button while the band plays and watch what changes on the staff.

How to play it. Sixteen eighths over two bars grouped 3+3+4+3+3. As before, count the groups and play on the first of each; the 4 in the middle is the turnaround of the pattern.

The band plays it on piano here; the step after next has it on guitar.

Step 4: Up to tempo, with the band

The whole band, at 120 beats a minute. Play along, then switch the band’s chord player off and take the part yourself.

Step 5: On the guitar

The same rhythm on the guitar. On guitar each chord is a strum or a pluck of a chord shape; a short chord is choked by easing the fretting hand off the strings.

Step 6: Two chords in a bar

Harder: now some bars have two chords, two beats each. The pattern keeps its rhythm and changes chord where the bar does: watch the staff for the hit that lands on beat 3.

All the accompaniment patterns

The pattern

Thumb and fingers, after John Prine. The thumb plays every beat on the low strings: the root, an inner string, the alternate bass, the inner string again. The fingers pinch a treble string with the thumb on 2 and 4 and add the string below it on the and after. In 3/4 the pinches are on 2 and 3.

It belongs in John Prine Fingerpicking, Boom-chick, Acoustic strum, Folk carol and Country train beat. Here it is in the john prine fingerpicking style with the whole band. Switch the other players off to hear it alone.

Step 1: Strum: downstrokes on the beat

Start with something simpler. One ringing downstroke on every beat. The first strum to learn, and the usual one for a slow song.

This is a pattern of its own: the lesson on it takes it further. Here it is only a step on the way, slowly. The drums keep time with you; switch the others on when it is steady.

Step 2: Boom-chick / oom-pah-pah

Short chords on the beats the bass leaves free: 2 and 4 in 4/4, 2 and 3 in a waltz. Goes with the Root and fifth bass line.

This is a pattern of its own: the lesson on it takes it further. Here it is only a step on the way, slowly. The drums keep time with you; switch the others on when it is steady.

Step 3: Fingerpicking: thumb, pinch-and, slowly

Now the pattern itself. Compare it with the step before: press each button while the band plays and watch what changes on the staff.

How to play it. The thumb plays every beat: root, an inner string, the alternate bass, the inner string. On 2 and 4 a finger pinches a treble string together with the thumb, and on the and after it plays the string below. Get the thumb going alone first; it must not stop when the fingers join.

Step 4: Up to tempo, with the band

The whole band, at 100 beats a minute. Play along, then switch the band’s chord player off and take the part yourself.

Step 5: Two chords in a bar

Harder: now some bars have two chords, two beats each. The pattern keeps its rhythm and changes chord where the bar does: watch the staff for the hit that lands on beat 3.

Step 6: In 3/4

The same pattern in a waltz: three beats to the bar. Listen for what it keeps and what it drops when the bar is a beat shorter.

All the accompaniment patterns

The pattern

The same thumb on every beat: root, inner string, alternate bass, inner string. The fingers pinch with it on beat 1, then play between the thumb’s notes: the and of 2, the and of 3, the and of 4.

It belongs in John Prine Fingerpicking, Boom-chick, Acoustic strum, Folk carol and Country train beat. Here it is in the john prine fingerpicking style with the whole band. Switch the other players off to hear it alone.

Step 1: Fingerpicking: thumb, pinch-and

Start with something simpler. Thumb and fingers, after John Prine. The thumb plays every beat on the low strings: the root, an inner string, the alternate bass, the inner string again. The fingers pinch a treble string with the thumb on 2 and 4 and add the string below it on the and after. In 3/4 the pinches are on 2 and 3.

This is a pattern of its own: the lesson on it takes it further. Here it is only a step on the way, slowly. The drums keep time with you; switch the others on when it is steady.

Step 2: Fingerpicking: Travis pattern, slowly

Now the pattern itself. Compare it with the step before: press each button while the band plays and watch what changes on the staff.

How to play it. The same thumb on every beat. The fingers pinch with the thumb on beat 1, then play in between the thumb notes: the and of 2, the and of 3, the and of 4. Thumb and fingers alternate like two players.

Step 3: Up to tempo, with the band

The whole band, at 100 beats a minute. Play along, then switch the band’s chord player off and take the part yourself.

Step 4: Two chords in a bar

Harder: now some bars have two chords, two beats each. The pattern keeps its rhythm and changes chord where the bar does: watch the staff for the hit that lands on beat 3.

The pattern

The notes of the voicing one at a time in eighth notes, up to the top and back down, each left to ring.

It belongs in Piano ballad, Jazz ballad, Boom-chick, Acoustic strum, 12/8 doo-wop, Hymn (four parts) and Folk carol. Here it is in the piano ballad style with the whole band. Switch the other players off to hear it alone.

Step 1: Long notes

Start with something simpler. One held chord per bar (or per chord). Leaves the most room for a soloist.

This is a pattern of its own: the lesson on it takes it further. Here it is only a step on the way, slowly. The drums keep time with you; switch the others on when it is steady.

Step 2: Arpeggio, low and high

Eighth notes rocking between the lowest and the highest note of the voicing.

This is a pattern of its own: the lesson on it takes it further. Here it is only a step on the way, slowly. The drums keep time with you; switch the others on when it is steady.

Step 3: Arpeggio, up and down, slowly

Now the pattern itself. Compare it with the step before: press each button while the band plays and watch what changes on the staff.

How to play it. The notes of the chord one at a time in eighths, up and back down, each left to ring. Piano: one hand position per chord, using the pedal. Guitar: hold the whole chord shape and pick string by string.

The band plays it on piano here; the step after next has it on guitar.

Step 4: Up to tempo, with the band

The whole band, at 72 beats a minute. Play along, then switch the band’s chord player off and take the part yourself.

Step 5: On the guitar

The same rhythm on the guitar. On guitar each chord is a strum or a pluck of a chord shape; a short chord is choked by easing the fretting hand off the strings.

Step 6: Two chords in a bar

Harder: now some bars have two chords, two beats each. The pattern keeps its rhythm and changes chord where the bar does: watch the staff for the hit that lands on beat 3.

Step 7: In 3/4

The same pattern in a waltz: three beats to the bar. Listen for what it keeps and what it drops when the bar is a beat shorter.

All the accompaniment patterns

The pattern

Every chord played once and held until the next one. On the piano or organ it is four parts: the root in the left hand and three voices above it that move as little as possible from chord to chord. It follows the chart’s chords, so a carol written with a chord on every beat sounds like the hymnal.

It belongs in Hymn (four parts), Folk carol and Piano ballad. Here it is in the hymn (four parts) style with the whole band. Switch the other players off to hear it alone.

Step 1: Long notes

Start with something simpler. One held chord per bar (or per chord). Leaves the most room for a soloist.

This is a pattern of its own: the lesson on it takes it further. Here it is only a step on the way, slowly. The drums keep time with you; switch the others on when it is steady.

Step 2: Hymn: four parts, slowly

Now the pattern itself. Compare it with the step before: press each button while the band plays and watch what changes on the staff.

How to play it. Four parts: left hand plays the root; right hand plays three notes that move as little as possible to the next chord. Keep any note two chords share in the same finger, and move the others to the nearest note of the new chord.

Step 3: Up to tempo, with the band

The whole band, at 80 beats a minute. Play along, then switch the band’s chord player off and take the part yourself.

Step 4: Two chords in a bar

Harder: now some bars have two chords, two beats each. The pattern keeps its rhythm and changes chord where the bar does: watch the staff for the hit that lands on beat 3.

Step 5: In 3/4

The same pattern in a waltz: three beats to the bar. Listen for what it keeps and what it drops when the bar is a beat shorter.

The pattern

The montuno rhythm played the salsa pianist’s way: octaves in both hands with the chord’s other notes between. The top note rocks between two chord tones: 1, 2, the and of 2, the and of 3, the and of 4; then every off-beat. Unheard: check by ear.

It belongs in Son montuno. Here it is in the son montuno style with the whole band. Switch the other players off to hear it alone.

Step 1: Son montuno

Start with something simpler. A two-bar pattern of short chords. First bar (shown): 1, 2, the and of 2, the and of 3, the and of 4. Second bar: every off-beat. Here it is played as block chords, not the pianist’s broken octaves.

This is a pattern of its own: the lesson on it takes it further. Here it is only a step on the way, slowly. The drums keep time with you; switch the others on when it is steady.

Now the pattern itself. Compare it with the step before: press each button while the band plays and watch what changes on the staff.

How to play it. The montuno rhythm again, now in octaves: thumb and little finger on the top note, the chord between on the off-beats. Let the top note rock between two chord tones and keep every note short.

The band plays it on piano here; the step after next has it on guitar.

Step 3: Up to tempo, with the band

The whole band, at 100 beats a minute. Play along, then switch the band’s chord player off and take the part yourself.

Step 4: On the guitar

The same rhythm on the guitar. On guitar each chord is a strum or a pluck of a chord shape; a short chord is choked by easing the fretting hand off the strings.

Step 5: Two chords in a bar

Harder: now some bars have two chords, two beats each. The pattern keeps its rhythm and changes chord where the bar does: watch the staff for the hit that lands on beat 3.

  • Other comping rhythms in the Latin group: Bossa nova, Tango (habanera), Piano guajeo (broken octaves), Cha-cha.

Cha-cha

For piano or guitar, built up a step at a time.

This is a lesson on one comping rhythm the Backing Track band plays: Cha-cha. It is built up from 2 simpler patterns, one step at a time, and every step is played by the band and written out as it plays. How the examples work: press ▶ Play, switch players in and out with the buttons beside it, and read what the band will play on the staff underneath: the whole pass is written out when Play starts, before it sounds. The tempo slider at the bottom of the page slows everything down.

All the accompaniment patterns

The pattern

A chord on 2, then the cha-cha-cha: 3, the and of 3, and 4.

It belongs in Cha-cha. Here it is in the cha-cha style with the whole band. Switch the other players off to hear it alone.

Step 1: Quarter-note chords

Start with something simpler. The chord on every beat, held. On the piano the left hand adds the root underneath as each chord arrives: Let It Be, Imagine, Someone Like You.

This is a pattern of its own: the lesson on it takes it further. Here it is only a step on the way, slowly. The drums keep time with you; switch the others on when it is steady.

Step 2: Boom-chick / oom-pah-pah

Short chords on the beats the bass leaves free: 2 and 4 in 4/4, 2 and 3 in a waltz. Goes with the Root and fifth bass line.

This is a pattern of its own: the lesson on it takes it further. Here it is only a step on the way, slowly. The drums keep time with you; switch the others on when it is steady.

Step 3: Cha-cha, slowly

Now the pattern itself. Compare it with the step before: press each button while the band plays and watch what changes on the staff.

How to play it. A chord on 2, then cha-cha-cha: 3, the and of 3, 4. Keep the three short and even.

The band plays it on piano here; the step after next has it on guitar.

Step 4: Up to tempo, with the band

The whole band, at 112 beats a minute. Play along, then switch the band’s chord player off and take the part yourself.

Step 5: On the guitar

The same rhythm on the guitar. On guitar each chord is a strum or a pluck of a chord shape; a short chord is choked by easing the fretting hand off the strings.

Step 6: Two chords in a bar

Harder: now some bars have two chords, two beats each. The pattern keeps its rhythm and changes chord where the bar does: watch the staff for the hit that lands on beat 3.

How it relates to the other patterns

  • Builds on: Quarter-note chords, Boom-chick / oom-pah-pah.
  • The same idea elsewhere in the band: Cha-cha (bass line), Cha-cha (drum groove), Tumbao (conga part).
  • Plays with, in cha-cha: Cha-cha (bass line), Cha-cha (drum groove), Tumbao (conga part).
  • Other comping rhythms in the Latin group: Bossa nova, Tango (habanera), Piano guajeo (broken octaves), Son montuno.
